strategy.summary: Mechanik Tauvelt GmbH is an owner-led Austrian family machinist (45 staff, financially sound). It is our single approved source for the duplex pump shaft part:320012, under framework ctr:4600070260 with prices fixed per calendar year. Across three renewals it asked for increases and settled for cuts, so the price has fallen every year. Real cost drivers rose over the last 12 months (bars, labour, alloy), but bars and alloy have eased since mid-2026. We are a small account for it (about 1.9% of its turnover), and its sales director says it is reviewing small accounts. Our forecast volume is rising. It asked us for 10-day payment against a cash discount. We pay late on most invoices. The owner offered to open his calculation and expects partnership in return for holding the old price in 2022. Leverage is balanced. Win by trading volume, faster and punctual payment, and length for price restraint, not by squeezing. Evidence is thin: no should-cost, no quotes, no alternative source.

Real input rises in bars, labour and alloy after three consecutive cuts. It needs at least a fair hearing on cost.

No other approved source and a 100% quota. We own the tooling, but no alternative has been qualified.
Small-account review: we are a small customer and the supplier is sound enough to walk away.
Plant holiday shutdown at year end. January call-offs are needed early.

price_view.reasoning: Three consecutive cuts and real driver rises leave limited further downside. Its history of settling far below its ask and recent material easing argue against more than a modest increase. A realistic target is roughly flat, using payment, volume and length trades. No should-cost exists, so the open-book walkthrough is key.

strategy.writer_notes: Write personally to the owner and respectfully. Open with the volume growth, the payment answer and acceptance of the open-book walkthrough as one partnership package. Keep the easing material records for later rounds. Hold the faster-payment trade for the last step. Recognise that its quality is excellent. Mention punctual payment on our side.

findings.text: No should-cost, no quotes and no RFQs exist for part 320012, so we cannot say how far its price sits above full cost. Any margin judgement rests only on index movements and price history; the evidence is thin.
Price history shows a steady fall: 111.85 (2023), 107.34 (2024), 106.98 (2025) and 105.87 since 2026-01-01. That is -5.3% since 2023. Current orders are at 105.87, which anchors any increase.

Weighted 12-month driver moves favour the supplier, about +4.2% on the price in total. Labour +2.7% at weight 0.32 adds about +0.85%. Cold-drawn bars +12.3% at weight 0.20 adds about +2.45%. Alloy surcharge 1.4404 +5.9% at weight 0.16 adds about +0.95%. Power -3.7% at weight 0.01 takes off about -0.04%. The remaining ~31% of cost has no assigned driver.

Short-term momentum has turned in our favour. Bars are -2.3% since their 2026-06 peak and the alloy surcharge is -5.5% from 2026-06 to 2026-09. Since 2026-06, material is easing, which offsets about 1.3% of the yearly rise. On the longer view, bars are -7.5% against their 2022 high and alloy is -13% against its 2023 peak. Those long-run comparisons are not checkable.

The material driver has a grade mismatch. The part is duplex 1.4462, but the alloy surcharge tracked is for 1.4404, with Cr and Mo held at fixed values. The surcharge figure therefore only approximates the real material cost.

The supplier has a pattern of asking for increases and settling for cuts. Across 3 renewals it asked +1.4% on average and settled -1.8%; last time it asked +2.6% and settled -1.0%. Expect a 2027 ask of roughly +3–4%. A realistic outcome is flat to about +1.5%. Volume (1552 vs 1354) and payment terms could pull this to flat or slightly below.

Faster payment (10 days with cash discount)

Our late payment (87% of invoices late) weakens our position
Duplex grade cost may have risen more than the 1.4404 proxy shows

findings.text: Owner-led family firm (founded 1979, 45 staff, turnover 5-10 M EUR). The owner negotiates personally and thinks in terms of relationship and reciprocity. He reminded us that in 2022 they held the old price for a quarter and expects 'partnership in return'. Expect appeals to fairness. Disrespect or hard bluffs will likely backfire.

The owner offered an open-book walk-through of their calculation (hourly rates, material). This is a lever: it lets us test cost-driver claims against labour (+2.7%) and bar/alloy indices instead of accepting assertions. Alloy has already fallen 5.5% since 2026-06.

They want cash. They asked for payment within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount (2026-09-13). We currently pay late on 87% of invoices (avg 4.1 days after due), so faster, on-time payment is a cheap trade currency for price. The financials are sound (equity 38.8%, credit index stable at 240), so the request reflects a cash preference rather than distress.

Red flag: the sales director said they are reviewing small accounts and will focus on customers with volume. We are about 1.9% of their turnover and they are our single approved source for part 320012. Deprioritisation risk is real. Our forecast volume rises from 1354 to 1552 units, which is a strong counter-signal to offer.

History weakens their price position. In 3 renewals they settled on average 3.2 pp below their ask. The price has fallen 5.3% since 2023, to 105.87. Quality is excellent at 0 ppm. On-time delivery slipped to 92.3%, below the 95% target.

Operational style: they plan in an orderly way and ask for early call-offs around the holiday shutdown (23 Dec-6 Jan). The solar news is noise. Overall the evidence is moderate: only one direct statement each from the owner and from the sales director.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070260 covers only part:320012 (pump shaft HI duplex), runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (by 2027-04-01). Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, so by about 2 October 2026 for 2027. A late increase request has no contractual basis for 1 Jan 2027.

Payment terms are 30 days net, against our 60-day standard. Delivery is FCA, so freight is on us, with a 35-day lead time. The quality agreement sets a 95% on-time target and EUR 150 per supplier-caused complaint. On-time delivery is 92.3%, below the contract target and down from 95.8%. Quality is 0 ppm.

History of the annual renewals: the supplier asked -0.1%, +1.8% and +2.6% and settled at -4%, -0.3% and -1%. That is an average ask of +1.4% against an average settlement of -1.8%, a gap of about 3.2 pp. The unit price fell from 111.85 (2023) to 105.87 (2026). Every renewal ended below the supplier's ask and below the prior price.

Mutual dependency is lopsided both ways. We single-source the part (100% quota, approved since 2022), but we own the tooling, so the part could move. Our spend of about EUR 144k is roughly 1.9% of the supplier's turnover. Sales has said they are reviewing small accounts, and the supplier is financially sound. Thin evidence: there is no RFQ history and no second approved source.

Signals that give us trade currency: the supplier asked us to pay within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount, and the owner offered to open up its cost calculation. On the other side, it invokes having held the old price for a quarter in 2022, and we pay 4.1 days late on average.

findings.text: Quality is flawless: 0 ppm, 0 complaints, 0 QNs and no overdue 8D across all nine rolling scorecards (2024Q3-2026Q3) on about 1,350 pcs/year. The peer median is 457 ppm. This argues the supplier's case; defect cost to us is nil, and the EUR 150 chargeback clause has never triggered.

On-time delivery has slipped below the contractual 95% target. It was 95.5-100% through 2025Q3 and has been 92-92.3% since 2025Q4. The last 12 months show 2 of 26 receipts late, by about 9 days on average and 10 days at most. It is still class A green and well above the peer median of 84.6%. This is a modest, factual lever for terms (lead time, ppm/OTD commitment) rather than a strong price lever. The sample is very small: one late receipt moves the figure about 4 points.

Volume is growing. The forecast shared with the supplier is 1,552 pcs for the next 12 months against 1,354 ordered in the last 12 months (+14.6%). Received quantities rose steadily from 1,107 to about 1,354. This is our main for-us argument, especially since its sales director said they will focus on customers with volume. Our spend is small for them (about EUR 144k, 1.9% of their turnover).

Our forecasts have been reliable and slightly conservative. Snapshots from 2024-09 onward predicted about 1,354-1,456 pcs, close to the 1,350-1,357 actually ordered per year. This makes the 1,552 outlook credible as a binding-volume trade.

Price has fallen each year: 111.85 (2023), 107.34 (2024), 106.98 (2025), 105.87 now, a cut of 5.3% overall. The current 105.87 anchors any request. The steady cuts also support the supplier's partnership narrative.
Order handling is clean: few rush or changed lines (3 each), quantity variance of 0.05%, and the latest POs were confirmed on the requested dates.

arguments.text: Three consecutive price cuts while our real costs rose: 111.85 to 105.87 (-5.3%) since 2023, despite asking for increases each time. We have absorbed enough; this year we need a correction, not another cut.

Cost drivers for a 1.4462 duplex shaft: cold-drawn bars +12.3% in 12 months (weight about 20%), labour +2.7% (about 32%), alloy surcharge +5.9% (about 16%). Weighted, that is roughly +4% on the cost base before margin.
Flawless quality: 0 ppm and 0 complaints across all scorecards, class A green. The customer never pays a chargeback or a defect cost with us.
Partnership: in 2022 we kept supplying at the old price for a quarter. We expect fairness in return.
The customer pays late on 87% of invoices (average 4.4 days past due), which effectively finances them at our cost.
Open book: the owner offered to walk them through our hourly rates and material costs, so our ask is transparent.

weak_points: Bars and alloy have eased since mid-2026 (bars -2.3% from the June peak, alloy -5.5% within the year, -13% from the 36-month peak) and power is -43% versus 2022; our solar plant lowers energy cost further.
OTD has fallen from 95-100% to 92%, below the contractual 95% target.
History shows we settle far below our ask, so they will discount our opening.
Volume is rising (forecast 1552 vs 1354 ordered), which spreads our fixed cost; they will ask us to share that.
They own the tooling and could resource; our small-account talk is a weak threat because they are about 1.9% of our turnover and churning them costs us too.
Any increase depends on giving written notice at least 90 days before year end (clause 3.1), i.e. by early October. If we miss that, we have no contractual basis.
There is no should-cost data, so opening our book could also reveal our margin.
wants: Payment within 10 days (with a 2% cash discount), or at least punctual payment at 30 days.
A binding annual volume of about 1,500 pieces, or call-off commitments.
A 24-month extension of the framework beyond 2027-06.
Alternatively, an index clause on bars and alloy instead of a fixed price.
Early January call-offs placed before our shutdown.
red_lines: Not below 105.87 (flat) without a binding volume and faster payment.
No new chargeback above EUR 150 per complaint, and no ppm penalties beyond the current regime.
No price commitment longer than 12 months without an index clause.
red_team.opening: Thank the customer for a stable partnership with zero defects. Note that we accepted three cuts since 2023 while bars rose 12.3%, alloy 5.9% and labour 2.7%. Ask for +4.5% to about EUR 110.60 from 2027-01-01, with written notice given in time under clause 3.1. Offer the open-book walkthrough. Signal that we would hold the increase to around +2% in exchange for 10-day payment with a discount, a binding 1,500 pieces a year and a contract extension to 2029.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that the price has come down at each renewal, and we value that you kept supplying reliably throughout. Those settlements were agreed together, each time below your opening request, which shows they reflected what both sides found fair at the time. We start from the price we pay today. Our aim this year is not to press for another cut but to find a fair level, and to support it with things you have asked for: more volume, a longer commitment and faster, punctual payment.

We accept that bars, labour and alloy rose over the last twelve months, and we take that seriously. The picture has turned more recently, though: bar prices and the alloy surcharge have both come down since the middle of the year, and power is lower than a year ago. A weighted view based on current levels supports a much smaller effect than your estimate. A rising volume also spreads your fixed costs over more pieces. We would be glad to go through this with you using the actual index figures.

Your quality record is excellent, and we say so openly; it is a real reason we want to keep and grow this business with you. Delivery has been less steady: on-time performance has slipped below the target in our agreement, although it still compares well with other suppliers. We would like to work with you on call-off scheduling so that delivery matches your quality again.

We remember the support you gave by holding the old price for a quarter, and we appreciate it. We want to return that partnership in ways that matter to you: a growing, planned volume shared in our forecasts, a longer commitment that gives you planning security, and payment that is faster and on time.

That is a fair point, and we will fix it. Most of our payments arrive a few days late, rarely by much, but punctuality is our obligation. We are ready to commit to paying on time and to discuss your proposal of faster payment against a cash discount as part of this agreement.

Thank you for the offer to walk us through your calculation; we would like to take it up. Going through hourly rates and material together, using the current index levels, is the best way for both of us to reach a level that is fair and lasting.

press: We would be grateful if our review could reflect the recent easing in bar prices and the alloy surcharge, as well as current lower power costs.
Our forecast for the shaft is rising clearly, and we would like to agree how that growth in volume can be reflected in a fair unit price.
Could we look together at how call-off scheduling might bring on-time delivery back to the level in our quality agreement?
As our agreement fixes prices per calendar year, we would appreciate any proposed change in writing within the notice period set out in the contract.
We would welcome a date for the calculation walkthrough you kindly offered, so we can base our discussion on shared figures.
